title: Alma Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Alma wells have a 160-foot median depth, with typical finished-well costs of $16,400-$28,000.
h1: What Alma, Colorado Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Buying land near Alma means dealing mostly with mountain bedrock, not a predictable shallow alluvial aquifer. Records for permitted wells within five miles show a 160-foot median depth, a median reported yield of 7.0 gallons per minute, and a median static water level of 89 feet below the surface.

Those figures are useful for budgeting, but they do not guarantee what a new hole will find. Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, and nearby results can vary with the exact ridge, valley, fracture zone, and access conditions. Check the well records before you commit to a lot.

sections.heading: Alma well depth depends on the bedrock
sections.html:
The middle half of recorded Alma-area wells runs from 108 to 240 feet. That is a practical range to discuss with a driller, while recognizing that the records extend from shallow wells to a deepest reported depth of 1,002 feet. About 67% of wells fall between 100 and 300 feet, while 19% are under 100 feet.

Granite and gneiss create fractured-bedrock conditions. Water commonly comes from fractures rather than a uniform underground layer, so two lots close together can drill differently. The 90th percentile is 330 feet, which is a useful warning against pricing a project only from the median. Ask for a bid that explains added footage, casing, grout, access, and difficult drilling conditions.

sections.heading: Most Alma wells make usable household flow
sections.html:
Reported pump yields are generally stronger than the depth variation might suggest. The median is 7.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half runs from 5.0 to 10.0 gallons per minute. About 73% of reported wells produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 17% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute.

Only 1% report less than 1 gallon per minute, but a low-producing well can still affect a home if storage and recovery are limited. A yield test is more useful than a nearby address alone. Review the permitted use as well: 95% of the records are domestic or household wells. Colorado exempt household-use wells still have limits, including the 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit.

sections.heading: Alma water levels look stable in the available record
sections.html:
The reported static water level has a median of 89 feet below ground surface, with the middle half between 50 and 130 feet. Static level means the water stood in the well when measured; it is not the same as the pumping rate or the amount of water a well can sustainably deliver.

The decade comparison does not show a falling trend in this data. Median static water level was 90 feet in the 2010s and 90 feet in the 2020s. Only 271 wells report a static water level, so treat the series as a limited local reference rather than a guarantee for an unbuilt lot. A driller should consider nearby well logs, elevation, and the proposed well location.

sections.heading: Permit history shows long activity around Alma
sections.html:
The records include permits from the 1950s through a newest permit year of 2025. Permit volume was highest in the 2000s, with 736 permits, followed by the 1990s with 578. The database contains 2,737 wells, including 1,838 recorded as constructed.

Allen Drilling & Excavating Co., Inc. (Allen, Jack R.) appears most often, with 890 records. Five Star Inc. (Werner, Peter S.) has 196, and Whitewater Drilling Inc (Benkufski, John D.) has 180. These are permit-record patterns, not a guarantee of current availability or workmanship. Confirm licensing, scheduling, scope, and who will handle the DWR permit for a new well.

sections.heading: What an Alma well can cost to drill
sections.html:
For Alma's fractured mountain ground, the cost model uses a drilling rate of $65-$100 per foot. At the 160-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $10,400-$16,000. That is not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $16,400-$28,000 at the median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, additional casing or grout, and longer utility runs can change the bid. Since 13% of wells are between 300 and 600 feet and 1% exceed 600 feet, ask the contractor how the price changes if the first target depth does not produce enough water.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building near Alma
sections.html:
Low yield is not the only issue. Mapped environmental data within about 10 miles includes 11 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 2,889 historic mine features, and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped features do not prove contamination at a particular parcel, but they are reasons to review site history and test water after construction.

Ask for the well permit, construction report, pump test, and water-quality results for nearby properties. Septic setbacks, suitable soil, driveway access, electrical service, and a legal building location all matter before drilling. In an over-appropriated basin, water rights or an augmentation plan may also affect new use. Confirm the parcel's permit conditions with Colorado DWR rather than assuming a domestic well permits every intended use.

sections.heading: Use nearby records when buying an Alma lot
sections.html:
Start with wells on the same slope or drainage, not just a broad search around town. The records are concentrated in fractured-bedrock aquifers: 2,640 permits name unnamed or fractured bedrock, compared with 15 alluvial wells and 9 in glacial deposits. That makes the exact location especially important.

Compare lots near Fairplay, Blue River, Leadville, Leadville North, Breckenridge, and Copper Mountain only as regional context; geology and access can change quickly across mountain terrain. Before closing, have a Colorado well contractor review nearby depths, yields, water levels, and permit use. For a build, obtain a site-specific drilling estimate and coordinate the well with septic, driveway, trenching, and the house location.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Alma, Colorado?
faq.a: The median permitted-well depth within five miles of Alma is 160 feet. The middle half runs from 108 to 240 feet, and the 90th percentile is 330 feet. Records range to 1,002 feet. Most wells are in fractured mountain bedrock, so nearby well depths are useful for planning but cannot promise the depth on a particular lot.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Alma?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $65-$100 per foot in fractured granite and gneiss. At the 160-foot median depth, drilling the hole is about $10,400-$16,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is about $16,400-$28,000. Difficult access, deeper drilling, casing, grout, and longer utility runs can raise the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Alma wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 5.0 and 10.0 gallons per minute. About 73% of reported wells produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. About 1% report under 1 gallon per minute, so request a yield test and ask how storage will support the planned home.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Alma, Colorado?
faq.a: Well water should be tested rather than assumed safe. Within about 10 miles, mapped data includes 11 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 2,889 historic mine features, and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These maps do not establish contamination on your parcel. Test a new or transferred well for site-relevant contaminants and review nearby land uses and mine history.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Alma?
faq.a: The available decade data does not show a change in median static water level: it was 90 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 90 feet in the 2020s. The overall median is 89 feet, with a middle half from 50 to 130 feet. Only 271 wells report static levels, so this is a limited indicator, not a guarantee for a new well.
